PHASE 4 · ADVANCED PRIMARY CARE CLINICAL MANAGEMENT

Week 88 — Lesson 112: Psoriasis & Psoriatic Arthritis

FNP-level goal: Recognize psoriasis as a chronic multisystem inflammatory disease, distinguish a routine plaque flare from dangerous mimics, screen deliberately for psoriatic arthritis and major comorbidities, and coordinate skin, joint, and longitudinal primary-care management.

Learning Objectives

  • Recognize common psoriasis patterns and distinguish plaque psoriasis from important mimics such as tinea, dermatitis, drug eruptions, and infection.
  • Use a structured psoriasis assessment that includes location, symptoms, nail and scalp disease, body-surface burden, special-site impact, mental health, and prior treatment response.
  • Screen for psoriatic arthritis (PsA) through inflammatory symptoms, dactylitis, enthesitis, nail findings, and functional change; understand why no single test rules PsA in or out.
  • Address cardiovascular, metabolic, behavioral, inflammatory-bowel, and mental-health comorbidities as part of psoriasis care.
  • Recognize when topical care is reasonable, when dermatology or rheumatology referral is needed, and when infection, erythroderma, or severe systemic illness requires urgent evaluation.

Part 1 — Psoriasis Is a Systemic Inflammatory Disease

Psoriasis is often visible on the skin, but it is not merely a cosmetic rash. It is a chronic immune-mediated inflammatory disease that can affect skin, nails, joints, function, sleep, mood, and cardiometabolic risk. The FNP should avoid reducing severity to body-surface area alone: a smaller eruption on the hands, feet, face, genitals, scalp, or nails can have a disproportionate effect on work, intimacy, mobility, and quality of life.

Ask what the patient calls the condition, when it began, whether it is itchy, painful, fissured, bleeding, or disrupting sleep, and what treatment has helped or harmed. Ask about personal and family history, recent infections, new medicines, skin trauma, stress, tobacco, alcohol, pregnancy plans when relevant, and access barriers. A medication list is not clerical work here: some drugs and abrupt withdrawal of systemic corticosteroids can aggravate psoriasis in susceptible patients.

Part 2 — Recognize the Cutaneous Patterns

Plaque psoriasis commonly appears as well-demarcated erythematous plaques with scale. In darker skin tones, erythema may look violaceous, gray, or hyperpigmented rather than bright red; inflammation must not be underestimated because it looks different from textbook photographs. Scalp, extensor surfaces, gluteal cleft, and umbilicus are frequent sites.

Nail pitting, onycholysis, subungual change, and dystrophy may support psoriatic disease, but fungal infection can coexist or mimic nail psoriasis. Palms and soles may fissure and hurt even when the total body-surface area is small. Guttate, inverse, pustular, and erythrodermic patterns have different clinical appearances and risk profiles; do not force every presentation into a plaque-psoriasis label.

Part 3 — Differential Diagnosis Before Escalating Treatment

Tinea may have an advancing scaly border, but appearance alone can be misleading. Seborrheic dermatitis can overlap with scalp or facial psoriasis. Atopic or contact dermatitis, pityriasis rosea, secondary syphilis when clinically appropriate, cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, and drug eruptions may also enter the differential. If the morphology, distribution, response, or systemic context is atypical, pause before escalating immunosuppressive treatment and obtain diagnostic support or dermatology input.

A painful, warm, draining, rapidly progressive, or systemically symptomatic eruption is not a routine outpatient flare until infection and other urgent conditions have been considered. Never use a familiar diagnosis to explain away new danger signs.

Part 4 — Psoriatic Arthritis: Ask Every Time

PsA can cause irreversible joint damage, yet skin disease may be treated for years before anyone asks about joints. At psoriasis follow-up, ask about joint pain, morning stiffness, swollen joints, heel pain, tendon pain, a whole swollen finger or toe, reduced range of motion, back pain with inflammatory features, fatigue, and change in function. Ask patients to point to the painful area; location and pattern matter more than the word arthritis alone.

High-value PsA clues include dactylitis (a diffusely swollen digit), enthesitis (inflammation at tendon or ligament insertions, often at the heel), nail pitting or onycholysis, inflammatory stiffness, and asymmetric or distal joint involvement. A validated screening tool such as PEST can support case finding, but it is not a diagnosis and should not replace a focused history and examination.

Part 5 — There Is No Single PsA Test

PsA is a clinical diagnosis supported by the pattern of skin, nail, joint, entheseal, and axial findings. Laboratory tests, radiographs, ultrasound, or MRI may help answer specific questions or evaluate alternatives, but no isolated blood test excludes PsA. Normal inflammatory markers do not erase a convincing inflammatory history. Conversely, a positive screening questionnaire should lead to clinical assessment and referral—not an automatic disease label.

When inflammatory arthritis is suspected, prompt rheumatology evaluation protects function. Delayed referral can mean preventable structural damage. The FNP role is to recognize the pattern, document objective findings and functional impact, manage safe symptom support within scope, and coordinate rather than attempt to replace disease-modifying specialty care.

Part 6 — Comorbidity Care Is Core Care

Psoriasis is associated with PsA, obesity, metabolic syndrome, dyslipidemia, hypertension, insulin resistance or diabetes, tobacco and alcohol exposure, cardiovascular disease, inflammatory bowel disease, and depression or anxiety. This does not mean every patient will develop each condition, and it does not justify assumptions. It means the primary-care visit should intentionally review prevention and monitoring rather than treating the plaque in isolation.

Use routine evidence-based screening and individualized risk assessment for blood pressure, weight, glycemic status, lipids, mood, substance use, and cardiovascular risk. Ask about bowel symptoms, eye symptoms, and family history when the clinical context suggests inflammatory comorbidity. Shared decisions should account for the patient’s values, access, and cultural understanding of visible skin disease.

Part 7 — Treatment Thinking: Match the Plan to Site, Severity, and Safety

Many patients with limited disease can benefit from topical therapy, moisturization and scale management, trigger review, and a follow-up plan. Potency and vehicle should fit the body site and diagnosis; thin or intertriginous skin deserves different caution than thick plaques on elbows or knees. Teach quantity, duration, adverse-effect monitoring, and when to step down or return. A vague instruction to use a cream as needed is not a safe treatment plan.

More extensive disease, difficult special sites, major quality-of-life impairment, refractory disease, diagnostic uncertainty, or consideration of phototherapy, systemic therapy, or biologics warrants dermatology collaboration. Systemic treatment requires indication-specific screening, vaccination and infection-risk review, monitoring, and coordination with specialists. The FNP should not promise that a systemic immunomodulator is risk-free or interchangeable with another therapy.

Part 8 — Avoid the Systemic Corticosteroid Trap

Systemic corticosteroids are not a routine long-term solution for psoriasis flares. Withdrawal can precipitate serious rebound disease in susceptible patients, while ongoing exposure carries well-known metabolic, bone, mood, infection, and other risks. If a patient has received systemic corticosteroids for another indication, document the context and coordinate a safe plan rather than abruptly stopping or reflexively extending therapy.

Part 9 — Urgent and Emergency Red Flags

Urgent evaluation is appropriate for rapidly generalized erythema with systemic symptoms, widespread pustules, fever, dehydration, severe pain, unstable vital signs, suspected serious skin infection, or a patient who appears toxic. Erythrodermic or generalized pustular presentations can impair temperature and fluid regulation and may be life-threatening. Patients with acutely hot, swollen joints, fever, inability to bear weight, or marked functional loss also need prompt assessment for septic arthritis or other urgent causes rather than an assumed PsA flare.

Part 10 — FNP Case: Skin Disease With Hidden Joint Disease

A 46-year-old patient with limited scalp plaques says the skin problem is controlled but reports morning finger stiffness, heel pain, and one toe that becomes swollen for days. The modest visible plaque burden should not reassure the clinician. Nail examination, joint and enthesis assessment, functional history, a PsA screener when useful, and prompt rheumatology referral are appropriate. The patient may have limited skin disease and clinically important joint disease at the same time.

Part 11 — FNP Case: A Dangerous Assumption

A patient with known psoriasis develops diffuse painful redness, fever, and malaise after stopping a systemic medication. Calling this a routine flare and changing an outpatient topical product would be unsafe. The combination of widespread inflammation and systemic illness requires urgent evaluation, medication reconciliation, and specialist coordination.

FNP High-Yield Framework

  1. Confirm the pattern: morphology, distribution, skin tone, scalp/nail involvement, symptoms, and mimics.
  2. Measure impact: body surface area plus special sites, sleep, pain, fissures, function, mood, and treatment burden.
  3. Screen joints every time: inflammatory stiffness, swelling, dactylitis, enthesitis, heel pain, nails, and functional decline.
  4. Screen systems: cardiovascular and metabolic risk, mood, smoking/alcohol, and symptoms that suggest inflammatory comorbidity.
  5. Choose safe escalation: topical detail for limited disease; dermatology for complex skin disease; rheumatology promptly for suspected PsA; emergency care for systemic or severe presentations.

Take-Home Summary

Psoriasis requires more than prescribing a topical agent. The FNP evaluates the skin accurately across skin tones, asks about joints at every relevant visit, identifies comorbidities and psychosocial harm, and makes a clear referral decision. PsA is a clinical pattern without a single rule-out test; earlier recognition and rheumatology care can protect long-term function. Severe generalized, pustular, infectious, or systemically ill presentations should not be managed as routine outpatient flares.

Educational note: This lesson supports clinical reasoning and does not replace individualized diagnosis, current prescribing information, local protocols, specialist guidance, or emergency evaluation when red flags are present.
